notes.meaning: The Philistines kept God's sacred chest in their land for seven months. Even though terrible sickness broke out wherever it went, they were slow to let go of what they thought was a great trophy. Sinners often prolong their own misery by refusing to give up what does not belong to them.

The Philistine leaders called together their pagan priests and fortune-tellers to ask how to return the ark properly. They realized the God of Israel was far too strong to fight against, but they did not know the right way to approach Him. Even people who do not know the true God often sense that holy things must be handled with care.

The priests warned them not to send the ark back empty, but to include a guilt offering. A guilt offering was a gift meant to make amends for an offense and turn away God's anger. They believed that if the people were healed afterward, it would prove that Israel's God had caused their suffering.

When the rulers asked what gift to make, the priests told them to craft five gold tumors and five gold rats. These matched the five rulers and main cities of Philistia, showing that all their leaders and people shared in the punishment. By modeling the very things that plagued them, they openly admitted their helplessness and sought God's mercy.

The priests told them to honor the God of Israel by admitting His power over them, their land, and their false gods. Swarms of rats had been ruining their crops while painful swellings struck their bodies. Honoring God meant acknowledging that He was the true judge who had crushed their idols and the only one who could grant relief.

The priests reminded the people of how Pharaoh and the Egyptians stubbornly refused to listen to God, only to be shattered by plagues. They warned that hardening their hearts would only lead to greater disaster. Wise people learn from the past rather than repeating the mistakes of others.

The priests gave directions to build a brand-new cart and hitch two mother cows that had never pulled a yoke. They also ordered the cows' nursing calves to be taken away and shut up in a barn. By natural instinct, mother cows would fight the yoke and try to run back to feed their young.

The ark was placed onto the cart, and the gold offerings were put in a small chest beside it. The Philistines did not dare open the sacred chest itself because they feared God's anger. Then they set the wagon on the road without any human driver to guide it.

The Philistines set up a test to find out if their troubles were really from the Lord. If the untrained cows went against nature and walked straight toward the Israelite town of Beth-shemesh, God was guiding them. If they turned back toward home, the Philistines would conclude that their sickness had just been bad luck.
The Philistines carried out the priests' plan exactly. They hitched the two nursing cows to the new cart and penned up their calves at home. They were ready to watch what would happen next.

The men placed the ark of the Lord on the wagon alongside the box containing the golden rats and tumor models. God had commanded His people to carry the ark only on poles, but He overlooked the Philistines' method because they did not know His law. They showed the holy chest the best respect their customs knew.

The cows walked straight down the road toward Beth-shemesh without turning to the left or right. They were mooing for their calves the whole way, showing their motherly pull, yet an unseen hand kept them moving forward. The five Philistine rulers followed behind in amazement until they reached the border.

The people of Beth-shemesh were cutting wheat down in the valley during the late spring harvest. When they looked up from their work and saw the ark coming, their hearts overflowed with joy. The return of God's presence brought far greater celebration than any plentiful harvest could bring.

The cart rolled into a field owned by a man named Joshua and stopped beside a large rock. The people chopped up the wooden wagon for firewood and offered the two cows as a burnt sacrifice to the Lord. They gladly gave up valuable animals and timber to thank God for His return.

Levites living in the town lifted down the ark and the chest of gold and set them on the great rock. Because Beth-shemesh was a town assigned to the tribe of Levi, qualified men were present to handle the sacred chest properly. The people then offered more sacrifices and shared meals of thanksgiving before God.

The five Philistine rulers watched from a distance until the ark was safely received and sacrifices were made. Having witnessed clear proof that the God of Israel had led the cows, their questions were answered. They returned to Ekron that same day, fully convinced of the Lord's power.

The writer lists the five major Philistine cities that sent back a gold tumor as a guilt offering: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Each city sent one image to make amends for mistreating God's ark. This public gift stood as a lasting record that Israel's God had brought their whole nation low.

The golden rats were sent not just for the five walled cities, but also for all the small farming villages that had suffered from the plague of rodents. The large rock where the ark had rested remained in Joshua's field for many years. It served as a lasting landmark to remind future generations of what God had done.

Joy turned to grief when some men of Beth-shemesh let curiosity replace reverence and looked inside the ark. God's law strictly forbade anyone from looking directly at the holy things, even the priests who carried them. God struck down seventy men for this bold disrespect, showing that His holiness must never be treated as common.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars and translations conclude that seventy men died, viewing the reading of 50,070 found in some manuscripts as an early copying error, especially since Beth-shemesh was a small farming village.

notes.meaning: Terrified by the sudden death of their neighbors, the men cried out asking who could possibly stand before such a holy God. Instead of confessing their own sin and lack of respect, they wanted to send the ark away so they would feel safe again. People often try to push God away when His purity exposes their shortcomings.

The men of Beth-shemesh sent messengers to the nearby hill town of Kiriath-jearim, asking them to come down and take the ark. Kiriath-jearim was a fortified town on higher ground and sat further away from the Philistine border. The sacred chest would rest there safely for many decades until King David brought it up to Jerusalem.
